summary:
BARA is an interactive web tool that helps students and environmentally curious people explore changes in forest and land fires, haze, and near-surface particle pollution in Sumatra and Kalimantan, Indonesia.

Using NASA FIRMS MODIS fire detections and MERRA-2 aerosol data, BARA combines a monthly 3D map with regional trend charts and a local fire-trend tool. Users choose a topic, place, and year, then investigate patterns across 2003–2025.

BARA addresses the "Earth System Trend Detective" challenge by showing what changed, where, how quickly, and how strong the statistical evidence is. Our main analysis compares July–October conditions across 23 years. Fire detections showed clearer downward trends than the pollution indicators, although conclusions remain sensitive to the short record and analysis choices.

Severe fire episodes attract attention, but individual events cannot reveal long-term change. BARA makes NASA’s open data easier to explore and helps users distinguish an extreme year from a lasting trend while understanding uncertainty.
details:
What BARA does

BARA is an interactive web tool for exploring changes in forest and land fires, atmospheric haze, and estimated near-ground fine-particle pollution in Sumatra and Kalimantan, Indonesia. It helps students and people interested in the environment investigate a question: how have these indicators changed over time, and how strong is the evidence for a trend?

Users choose a topic, place, and year, then explore a monthly 3D map covering 2003–2025. The Findings section presents regional trend charts, while a regency-level tool lets users calculate local fire-detection trends.

Data and Analysis

BARA uses NASA FIRMS MODIS Terra and Aqua active-fire detections, MERRA-2 aerosol optical depth (AOD) at 550 nm, and surface aerosol components used to estimate PM₂.₅. Rainfall, soil wetness, forest loss, and ocean-climate indices provide additional context.

The map includes all months. Our main regional analysis compares 23 July–October summaries, using Sen’s slope to estimate change rates and Mann–Kendall to assess trend significance. The Hamed–Rao autocorrelation adjustment did not change those results.

Fire detections showed clearer downward trends than the pollution indicators. Individual tests identified declining AOD in Kalimantan, but no statistically clear PM₂.₅ trend in either region. These findings remain exploratory: pollution results depend partly on the months selected, and none of the six trends remained significant after a Holm multiple-testing adjustment.

Why Sumatra and Kalimantan

Major fire and haze episodes in Sumatra and Kalimantan, including the 2015 fires, motivated our choice of study areas. Both regions contain extensive peatlands, making peat burning an important part of the environmental context. Available satellite and reanalysis records allow us to examine changes during 2003–2025. Comparing the regions also helps us investigate whether their fire and pollution trends differ.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Severe fire episodes attract attention, but one extreme year cannot reveal a long-term pattern. BARA makes NASA’s open data easier to explore and helps users distinguish an individual event from a trend across decades.

Its current purpose is environmental learning and historical investigation. Future work could examine possible explanations for the patterns, compare pollution estimates with independent observations, and support the development of seasonal preparedness tools.

Technology

We used Python for data processing and statistical analysis, Three.js for the 3D map, and D3.js for charts. Vercel hosts the frontend. Cloudflare Workers, D1, R2, and KV support backend services, regional queries, and data storage. Workers AI provides labeled plain-language explanations of computed results.

Creativity and Design Choices

BARA turns environmental measurements into a guided investigation. Users move from one place and year to a longer record, with maps and explanations helping them interpret the evidence.

We prioritized accessible language, consistent comparisons, and transparent limitations. Fire detections represent observed burning rather than separate fires or burned area. AOD describes aerosol loading throughout the atmospheric column, while estimated surface PM₂.₅ describes fine particles near the ground. Both pollution indicators come from MERRA-2 and are not independent checks. BARA describes historical patterns without claiming to establish their causes, measure personal exposure, or predict future fires.
